extracted.intended_audience: orators, students of classical rhetoric, and writers/teachers of wit and humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and taxonomy for composing and judging wit in oratory according to Cicero (Caesar Strabo's account in De Oratore II.216-290). Covers a two-branch classification of jokes, subtypes, necessary conditions for success, forbidden targets, and diagnostic questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cavillatio (de re / facetiae in re)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor of 'thing', situation, or sustained discourse; pervades a whole speech, character sketch, or anecdote. Cannot be fully extracted in a single line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for situational or extended humor that depends on context, narrative, or characterization rather than a single verbal turn. Expect development across sentences; not reducible to a one-line quip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dicacitas (de dicto / facetiae in dicto)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor of 'word' — the witticism, the sharp short remark. Lives or dies in a single phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for concise epigrams, repartee, and one-liners. Success depends on wording and immediate effect; longer explanation will usually ruin it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguum (pun / double meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pun or double meaning; technically admired but regarded as the lowest form of wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicero describes it as 'not so much witty as adroit' — clever wordplay is acceptable but can be seen as lightweight. Use sparingly and technically; avoid relying on puns as sole resource for sustained wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inopinatum (violation of expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying what is contrary to expectation; a thwarted expectation makes us laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central mechanism of much successful wit: lead the audience toward one expectation and subvert it with the line. Must be pertinent (arise from the matter at hand) and often benefits from brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegoria / per metaphoram (extended figurative play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended figurative play or allegory used for humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer figurative constructions can produce clever, layered humor but risk losing audience if overextended or obscure; should still relate to the occasion and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironia (saying the opposite of what one means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying the opposite of what one means to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective when audience recognises the contrast between utterance and intended meaning; risk of misinterpretation if context or speaker's stance doesn't make the irony clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verba immutata (substituted word)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting one word for another with surprising effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise comes from unexpected lexical substitution; keep it brief and contextually sensible so the substitution feels apt rather than forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected proverb or quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploying a salty proverb or quotation in an unexpected context for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recognizable proverb or quote used out of place can amuse by juxtaposition; ensure audience recognises the source and that the deployment is pertinent to the matter at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-changes / paronomasia (phonetic alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slight phonetic alteration that produces a new sense (paronomasia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like puns, phonetic play can be clever but is a lower, technical form of wit; best used sparingly and where it suits the speaker's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratio facete (humorous anecdote)
rubrics_metrics.description: The well-told humorous anecdote with vivid characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires good storytelling: vivid detail, timing, and characterisation. As a situational form it typically spans multiple sentences and relies on context and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitatio (mimicry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimicry of voice, manner, or character for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical or vocal imitation can be powerful in performance but must respect the speaker's dignity and audience sensibilities; can verge into ridicule if not handled deftly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature / contortio personae (exaggeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration of a real person's traits to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration highlights salient features for humor; avoid mean-spirited or cruel distortions that alienate the audience or attack universally beloved persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of unlikes
rubrics_metrics.description: Yoking the dignified and the trivial — comparing unlike things for comic contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective juxtaposition of high and low registers produces comic incongruity. Must be pertinent and not gratuitously insulting to audience values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissimulatio (pretended ignorance / Socratic irony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretending ignorance or innocence to expose absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strategic feigning of naivety to reveal contradictions in others' positions; requires subtlety so the audience sees the tactic rather than taking the ignorance at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretended seriousness about trivial things / trivializing the serious
rubrics_metrics.description: Feigning solemnity about trivial matters or making light of serious things for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be witty when it reveals absurd priorities, but risks offence if applied to genuinely grave subjects or to things the audience holds sacred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling a fable/story aimed at a present situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a fable or story targeted at current circumstances to produce humor or criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegorical stories can deliver pointed wit about a present case; clarity of parallel and pertinence to the occasion are crucial for the audience to make the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary conditions for good wit (grouped)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero's listed necessary conditions: brevitas, surprise, pertinence, relevance to speaker's character/dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are core tests: keep the dictum brief (brevitas), achieve surprise (violation of expectation), ensure the joke arises from the matter at hand (pertinence), and make sure the wit suits the speaker's dignity and role. Explanation will often kill the effect (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevitas (brevity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictum must be brief; explanation kills the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the line needs explanation to land, it fails as dicacitas. Prefer short, tightly-worded turns; in cavillatio, preserve economy and avoid over-exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (violation of expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We expect one thing and another is said; here our own disappointed expectation makes us laugh." (II.284)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design setups that steer expectations and then subvert them. Surprise must feel earned and relevant rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke must arise out of the matter at hand, not be dragged in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes should be organically connected to the ongoing subject or occasion. Irrelevant witticisms distract and undercut rhetorical goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to character of speaker (suitability/dignity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The orator's wit must suit his dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the speaker's status and persona; a joke that contradicts the speaker's role or dignity will seem inappropriate. Match tone and register to the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid joking about universally wretched or criminal things
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not joke about things universally regarded as wretched or criminal — you lose sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets that elicit moral disgust or pity are poor choices; laughing at such subjects alienates the audience and undermines the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid joking about the deeply pious
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not joke about the deeply pious — you appear impious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacrilegious or irreverent jokes toward deeply held religious sentiments risk offence and damage the speaker's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid joking about persons beloved by the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not joke about persons truly beloved by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attacking or ridiculing loved persons alienates listeners; such targets undermine rapport and can provoke backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contemptible trivialities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not joke about trivialities so small that the joke is contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheap or petty gibes that seem mean-spirited or beneath the speaker; such jokes lower the rhetorical tone and damage respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions (checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short diagnostic checklist for evaluating an instance of wit: Is the wit verbal or situational? Does the joke achieve Cicero's violation-of-expectation effect? Does brevity carry it, or does it require explanation? Does the joke fit the speaker's dignity and the occasion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to assess whether a proposed quip or anecdote is likely to succeed per Cicero's criteria. They function as quick pre-delivery filters to avoid common failures.
